Order in Council – Amending Schedule 1 to Add  the Mackenzie Valley Highway Project:  Explanatory Note   (This note is not part of the Order.)  Proposal On March 12, 2026, the Government of Canada announced the referral of the Mackenzie Valley Highway Project (MVH, or the Project) to the Major Projects Office (MPO) for further review and analysis. On June 24, 2026, the Government announced that it was initiating the process toward potential listing of the Project as a project of national interest under the Building Canada Act (BCA, or the Act).   The Project is a proposed approximately 800 kilometre four-season highway in the Northwest Territories. The highway would run the length of the Mackenzie River Valley, north of Wrigley, and pass near the communities of Tulita, Norman Wells and Fort Good Hope before connecting with the Dempster Highway, south of Inuvik. The Project would also involve the construction of new bridges, including across the Great Bear River near Tulita, and across the Liard and Mackenzie rivers near Fort Simpson.  Order The Governor in Council (GIC), pursuant to subsection 5(1) of the Act and on the recommendation of the Minister responsible under the Act, the President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada — the Honourable Dominic LeBlanc (the Minister) — amends Schedule 1 of the Act to add the Project as a national interest project, as specified in the Order in Council (Order) to which this Explanatory Note is appended.  Objective The objective of this Order is to facilitate the Project’s timely development by bringing it within the regulatory framework of the Act, based on the GIC’s determination that the Project is in Canada’s national interest and that the Act thus supplies an appropriate framework to structure applicable federal regulatory authorizations, ensure appropriate environmental safeguards, and meet Canada's constitutional obligations to Indigenous peoples.   At the same time, this Order acknowledges that the Project remains subject to treaty-based environmental assessment and regulatory processes in the Northwest Territories, including as implemented in the Mackenzie Valley Resource Management Act (MVRMA). This includes an environmental assessment by the Mackenzie Valley Environmental Impact Review Board (MVEIRB). Required federal and territorial authorizations, including a Conditions Document under the BCA, would only be issued if the project is approved following completion of the MVEIRB assessment process and as informed by that process.   The Building Canada Act Context Nation-building natural resource and infrastructure projects have long faced complicated, cumbersome and time-consuming federal regulatory processes. This has fostered uncertainty and deterred proponents from pursuing projects that could render vital social and economic benefits to Canada. The federal regulatory system for major projects has involved numerous authorizations and permitting decisions distributed among multiple federal agencies and departments, each requiring separate applications from project proponents, and entailing multiple, often disjointed processes of consultation with Indigenous governments and organizations. The duration and complexity of this system can delay federal authorization of worthy project proposals for years and systemically limit the willingness of proponents to bring forward projects that enhance Canada’s economic growth, security, and prosperity.   Within this context, global shifts in geopolitics and security are contributing to new vulnerabilities for Canada’s North and Arctic. Growing strategic competition, increasing international interest in Arctic resources and transportation corridors, and easier access are reshaping the region. Relative to other key Arctic jurisdictions, Northern Canada has lower levels of infrastructure development and economic activity, including infrastructure that is vital for sovereignty and autonomy. As other countries seek to advance their economic, security, and geopolitical interests in the North, Canada faces greater pressure to strengthen Northern infrastructure and protect its strategic interests.   Accordingly, Canada must act ambitiously to grow domestic economic resources, connect communities and improve transportation system resilience, and strengthen its ability to project and demonstrate its sovereignty in the region. Building confidence in Canada’s ability to develop infrastructure and major natural resource projects in the North, in partnership with territorial and Indigenous partners, is foundational to these objectives.   The BCA was enacted by Parliament on June 26, 2025, to provide a simplified, direct, timely and comprehensive process to secure federal regulatory authorization for projects determined to be of national interest to Canada. The Act provides a means to advance major infrastructure and natural resource projects in Canada. It enables the GIC to determine that certain projects are of such importance to Canada that they warrant access to a special regulatory framework that prioritizes streamlining, enhanced coordination, and efficiency.   Application of the Act occurs within the framework of Canada’s respect for Aboriginal and treaty rights as recognized and affirmed by section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982; Canada’s duty to consult with Indigenous peoples; its commitment to reconciliation; and its respect for the rights set out in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. Crown-Indigenous consultation is explicitly required to inform key decisions taken under the Act, including decisions to list national interest projects. These decisions can be made only after Canada has met its duty to consult and, where appropriate, accommodate Indigenous peoples whose Aboriginal and treaty rights may be adversely affected by the carrying out of the projects to which the decisions relate.   The Act also recognizes a commitment to working in partnership with Indigenous peoples and envisages opportunities for Indigenous participation in major projects as proponents, stakeholders, and investors. The Act identifies the extent to which a project can advance the interests of Indigenous peoples as one of the key factors relevant to the GIC’s determination of whether a project is in the national interest, and consultation with Indigenous governments and organizations prior to a listing decision facilitates early involvement in project development. It allows for Indigenous perspectives to inform whether a project is in Canada's national interest and enables Indigenous governments and communities to identify key issues and opportunities early, helping to inform subsequent project development and regulatory processes.  Finally, the Act reflects Canada’s commitment to safeguard the natural environment – including through the mitigation of potential effects of project development on critical species, habitats, and marine and terrestrial ecosystems – and to meet the challenges of climate change.   MPO, as a Special Operating Agency within Canada’s Privy Council Office, supports the Minister in the administration of the Act.  Applying the BCA in Canada’s Territories Across Canada’s territories, environmental assessment and regulatory review processes are governed by resource management regimes established through modern treaties. For example, these include the Yukon Umbrella Final Agreement, the Nunavut Land Claims Agreement, the Gwich'in Comprehensive Land Claim Agreement, the Sahtu Dene and Métis Comprehensive Land Claim Agreement, the Tlicho Land Claims and Self-Government Agreement, and the Inuvialuit Final Agreement (IFA). These resource management regimes are implemented under federal legislation, including Mackenzie Valley Resource Management Act (MVRMA), Yukon Environmental and Socio-economic Assessment Act, and Nunavut Planning and Project Assessment Act. These statutes are not included under Schedule 2 of the BCA and their applicable requirements are not replaced as a result of listing under the BCA of a project in the territories.   Resource Co-management in the Northwest Territories   In the Northwest Territories, an integrated co-management regime for environmental assessment, land and water management, and regulatory decision-making is established under the MVRMA. These treaty-based assessments support Indigenous participation in decision-making and provide independent processes to assess the environmental, social, cultural, and economic effects of proposed developments. Under this regime, the MVEIRB conducts environmental assessments and provides recommendations to responsible territorial and federal ministers, who make final decisions in accordance with the legislation.   Benefits of listing a project under the BCA in the Northwest Territories   The BCA operates harmoniously withthe treaty-based assessment process in the Northwest Territories. While listing a project under the BCA does not alter or predetermine the statutory requirements or outcome of those processes, listing can provide significant benefits. Notably, listing a project under the BCA formally identifies it as a project of national interest, establishing an important signal regarding the Government of Canada’s commitment to the project and its strategic importance. In this way, a listing decision acknowledges a project’s essential contribution to objectives that would benefit Canada, in alignment with the foundation of the BCA.   In application, a listing decision streamlines the process for the Government of Canada to consider the recommendations of MVEIRB’s environmental assessment by allowing the Minister responsible for the BCA to participate as a responsible federal minister under the MVRMA. For BCA-listed projects, the Minister assumes a role as a responsible minister under that process, charged with informing the response to MVEIRB’s Report of Environmental Assessment in relation to federal authorizations for statutes listed under Schedule 2 of the BCA, replacing what would otherwise be multiple federal ministerial decisions. This change simplifies a project’s approval process by reducing the number of federal ministers required to approve the Report, while preserving the role and expertise of federal departments in providing advice and guidance.  Further, listing establishes a streamlined framework for the issuance of federal authorizations in the event of project approval at the conclusion of the MVEIRB process. Specifically, the listing decision results in deemed fulfillment of substantive prerequisites to the release of federal permits and authorizations listed in Schedule 2 of the Act. As a result, if a project is approved at the conclusion of the treaty-based assessment process, federal authorizations can be issued more efficiently and with reduced regulatory duplication. The MVEIRB environmental assessment is the principal forum through which information relevant to support subsequent federal regulatory decisions is collected and considered. This includes baseline environmental conditions, impacts on fish and fish habitat, navigable waters, species at risk, Indigenous rights and interests, mitigation measures, monitoring requirements, and proposed accommodation measures. Through extensive Indigenous consultation, public participation, and technical review, the MVERIB environmental assessment therefore establishes an evidentiary record upon which federal regulators can rely.   Additionally, in the event of project approval following the MVEIRB environmental assessment, the Act enables federal regulatory processes listed under Schedule 2 of the BCA to be consolidated in support of a single authorization from the Minister responsible under the BCA. This single authorization, the Conditions Document, defines the federal regulatory conditions under which project construction and operation can occur. In the Northwest Territories, these conditions are developed based on outcomes of the treaty-based assessments and consultations with Indigenous governments and organizations. In this way, MVEIRB recommendations that require federal authorizations within the scope of the BCA are addressed in a consolidated manner through the Conditions Document after the completion of the MVRMA process. Listing thus establishes a clear path from the MVEIRB environmental assessment to the project conditions, with the Minister responsible for the BCA playing a central role.   The consolidation of federal authorizations under a single framework benefits a project by streamlining the process for proponents and enabling a single coordinated process of consultation with Indigenous governments and organizations. This approach builds on consultation undertaken throughout the project's development, including consultation associated with the listing decision and consultation conducted during the MVEIRB’s environmental assessment and ministerial decision phases. Where consultation is required to support federal decision-making or the development of project-specific conditions, the BCA provides a mechanism for the consultation to be coordinated through a single federal process, led by the Minister responsible for the Act, rather than through multiple separate authorization processes.   This coordinated approach to consultation also reduces duplication, improves transparency, and provides greater clarity regarding how Indigenous government and community concerns are considered and addressed through project development, including through mitigation and accommodation measures. Rather than addressing similar issues through multiple federal authorization processes issued by different departments, project-specific conditions are consolidated within a single federal authorization via the Conditions Document. In the context of treaty-based assessment processes, this is an important benefit of the BCA given the range of responsible organizations and approvals needed to advance major projects.  Mackenzie Valley Highway Project and Proponent The Project is a proposed approximately 800 kilometre, four-season highway in the Northwest Territories. The highway would run the length of the Mackenzie River Valley, north of Wrigley, and pass near the communities of Tulita, Norman Wells and Fort Good Hope before connecting with the Dempster Highway, south of Inuvik. The Project would also involve the construction of new bridges, including across the Great Bear River near Tulita, and across the Liard and Mackenzie rivers near Fort Simpson.   The MVH would provide year-round road access to currently isolated communities, increase regional trade and tourism, encourage new mineral and resource exploration and development, and support Arctic sovereignty and defence objectives.  The Project, a public-use territorial highway with important defence and security benefits, is being advanced by the Government of the Northwest Territories (GNWT) as the proponent.  Regulatory Context for the Project The MVEIRB environmental assessment of the Mackenzie Valley Highway began in 2013. The original scope extended from Wrigley to the Dempster Highway near Inuvik but was narrowed in 2014 to the southern Wrigley–Norman Wells segment. Revised Terms of Reference were issued in 2015, and the GNWT submitted its Developer’s Assessment Report (DAR) for that segment in October 2023. Substantial engineering, environmental, Indigenous Knowledge, socio-economic and engagement work has since informed both project development and the ongoing environmental assessment.  In August 2026, the GNWT requested that the existing assessment be expanded to include the corridor north of Norman Wells to a connection with the Dempster Highway, south of Inuvik. The GNWT also requested an extension to March 31, 2027, to submit revised assessment materials addressing the expanded scope. The MVEIRB initiated its re-scoping process in August, with community and technical sessions held during Fall 2026 to inform revisions to the Terms of Reference and assessment workplan. The GNWT is preparing a revised DAR addressing the expanded corridor, with submission targeted before the end of March 2027.  As the proposed routing of the MVH does not enter the Inuvialuit Settlement Region (ISR), the Inuvialuit Regional Corporation (IRC) has advised that so long as the MVEIRB environmental assessment sufficiently assesses and mitigates any transboundary impacts to the ISR, the Project would not require screening under the IFA assessment regime.   Regulatory Requirements  While the list of required federal authorizations will be finalized as project design is advanced and recommendations from the MVEIRB are finalized, the MVH would require substantial federal authorizations for statutes listed under Schedule 2 of the BCA before construction can begin.   This is expected to include Fisheries Act authorizations for works that may cause serious harm to fish or fish habitat. Under the Fisheries Act, any activity that results in the death of fish or harmful alteration, disruption or destruction of fish habitat requires an authorization, supported by detailed offsetting plans, hydrological modelling, and fish‑passage design.   In addition to Fisheries Act requirements, the project is anticipated to trigger federal review under the Canadian Navigable Waters Act for bridge and major culvert crossings along the Mackenzie Valley corridor.   The MVH is also anticipated to require compliance with the Migratory Birds Convention Act (MBCA) and may require authorizations under the Species at Risk Act where project activities could affect listed wildlife species. For a linear project of this scale, federal regulators would require detailed nest avoidance protocols, timing windows, vegetation clearing restrictions, and monitoring programs to demonstrate compliance with the MBCA.   Under the BCA framework, all of these federal authorizations can be issued through a Conditions Document, provided approval of the Project following the MVEIRB environmental assessment. Additional federal authorizations could be identified following the MVEIRB review and would be addressed and issued by the Minister responsible for that Act (for statutes listed under Schedule 2 of the BCA), or additional federal Ministers for non-listed statutes, such as the Explosives Act.   Basis for the Governor in Council’s Determination Subsection 5(6) of the Act provides that when making a listing decision, the GIC may consider any factor that it considers relevant, including the extent to which a project can:             strengthen Canada’s autonomy, resilience and security;           provide economic or other benefits to Canada;           have a high likelihood of successful execution;           advance the interests of Indigenous peoples; and           contribute to clean growth and to meeting Canada’s objectives with respect to climate change.  The GIC’s decision-making is informed by Crown-Indigenous consultation completed by the responsible Minister pursuant to subsection 5(7) of the Act and as required by section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982. It is also informed by consultation with implicated provincial or territorial governments; by the Minister having consulted with other ministerial colleagues as he considers appropriate; and by the views of Canadians, including those who respond to publication of Notice of a potential listing decision in the Canada Gazette. In the case of the MVH, listing also requires written territorial consent, which has been provided by the GNWT.   The following reflects the GIC’s overall assessment of the merit in listing the Project. As elaborated in the sections below, the GIC’s view is that: The balance of relevant factors in ascertaining the potential benefits of the Project, as well as its limitations and potential impacts, points clearly in favour of recognizing the Project as one in Canada’s national interest, to be pursued as a matter of priority;The Project would provide critical support for Canada’s sovereignty and security through the development of significant infrastructure in Canada’s North, enabling a more resilient, connected Northern transportation system that supports an expanding Canadian military presence in the North and Arctic; The listing of the Project is informed by meaningful consultation with Indigenous peoples; consistent with the honour of the Crown; informed by the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples; and consistent with respect for Aboriginal and treaty rights; Subject to the outcome of the MVEIRB environmental assessment process, the MVH would require a suite of federal authorizations under Schedule 2 of the BCA;The Project would benefit from listing under the BCA as a signal regarding the Government of Canada’s commitment to the Project and its strategic importance, while enabling stronger federal coordination across a range of different organizations;All appropriate preconditions for the Project’s BCA listing have been met.   Analysis of National Interest Factors  Strengthening Canada’s autonomy, resilience, and security   The GIC has concluded that the Project presents a critical opportunity to strengthen Canada’s autonomy, resilience, and security. The Project would establish a strong foundation to enhance Canada’s presence and operational capabilities in the North and Arctic, while improving the resilience and security of northern communities. By creating a reliable transportation route connecting key regions in the Northwest Territories, the MVH would also support Canada’s defence and security objectives.  Canada’s North faces significant infrastructure challenges. According to Canada's 2025 National Infrastructure Assessment, historical under-investment, harsh climate and remote geography all contribute to challenges such as insufficient transportation infrastructure including roads and ports, short seasonal construction windows, and permafrost adaptation requirements. All-season road networks are limited, leaving many communities dependent on costly air transport, seasonal barges and sealifts, or winter ice roads. Many communities with existing road access such as Inuvik, Wrigley, and Fort Simpson do not have four season access due to their use of seasonal ferries and winter ice crossings of major rivers. As a result, these communities are cut off from the national highway network during the spring thaw and fall freeze periods.   Climate change is exacerbating these realities. According to the Government of Canada’s 2026 Changing Climate report, the Canadian Arctic has warmed at three times the rate of the global average since 1970, and the greater rate of warming will continue through the twenty-first century. During warmer months, drought conditions frequently lower the water levels in the Northwest Territories, threatening the viability of the seasonal barge transportation on the Mackenzie River, which is critical for community resupply. In winter, climate change is shortening the operational window and compromising the safety of the existing winter road network. Warmer temperatures, mid-season thaws, and thinner ice coverage can result in earlier closures of roads, load restrictions, and higher risks of vehicles becoming stranded.   These challenges have significant negative impacts on Canada, the Northwest Territories, and especially Sahtu, Beaufort Delta, and Dehcho region communities. The lack of reliable road access constrains economic opportunity and raises the cost of living and public services, creates challenges for community resilience, and limits Canada’s ability to exercise effective presence and sovereignty across its northern and Arctic territories.   The MVH would address these issues by providing year-round road access to a series of communities located across the Northwest Territories that currently do not have year-round access to the national highway network, including Norman Wells, Tulita and Fort Good Hope. Already road-connected Beaufort Delta communities would also benefit from improved road access through a significantly shorter and all-season route to Yellowknife and Edmonton. Finally, two isolated communities in the Sahtu region, Deline and Coleville Lake, would benefit from significantly reduced distances across which seasonal winter roads would need to be built. In total, over 10,000 people (approximately 22 percent of the Northwest Territories population) across 12 communities would benefit from improved transportation access. This includes 1,900 people in the Sahtu region who would gain access to an all-season road for the first time.  The Project would also improve the overall resilience of the Northwest Territories’ transportation system. In addition to providing a new all-season road to certain communities, it would reduce travel time between key population centres. For example, the Project would reduce travel distance between Yellowknife (the territory’s capital and largest municipality) and Inuvik (the territory’s second largest population centre) by approximately 1,300 kilometres. Similarly, the MVH would reduce the travel distance between Inuvik and Edmonton by an estimated 900 kilometers.   Critically, the MVH would use bridges for all river crossings, whereas the existing Dempster Highway relies on seasonal ferries and ice crossings for major river crossings, and is not a true all-season route, as it is closed for approximately 4 to 6 weeks per year in spring and fall. Barge transportation on the Mackenzie River for fuel and bulk goods has also become increasingly unreliable due to fluctuating water levels.   The highway would significantly improve the region's resilience against supply chain disruptions, including those driven by climate change, improving food and energy security in Canada's North while also supporting the region's response to natural disasters and other emergencies.  Further to enhancing the resiliency of the Northwest Territories’ and Canada’s transportation system, the Project would also provide key defence and security-related benefits for the nation. As Canada expands its military presence in the North, reliable, year-round ground access will become increasingly essential to future operational requirements. More resilient transportation infrastructure would support the movement of military personnel, equipment, fuel and other supplies during routine operations, emergency response, and domestic support operations.   Compared to Arctic peers and relative to the rest of Canada, Northern Canada has lower infrastructure and economic density. Canada’s North accounts for about 1.8 percent of Arctic Gross Domestic Product (GDP) across all countries with Arctic territory on a purchasing power parity-adjusted basis, while making up 28 percent of the area of the global Arctic region, according to the Arctic Council’s estimates. Domestically, the three territories account for only about 0.5 percent of Canada’s GDP, despite making up almost 40 percent of Canada’s total area. Relative to other countries with Arctic territory, Northern Canada has a less extensive transportation infrastructure network, contributing to lower levels of economic integration and development. Canada also has fewer Arctic seaports and paved airports, and those that exist are spread over a significant distance.  The Project would connect Yellowknife and Inuvik, which are sites of growing Department of National Defence and Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) presence. Both cities host North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD) Forward Operating Locations that will be expanded considerably as part of $32 billion in planned NORAD modernization investments over the next 15 years, as announced by the Government of Canada in March 2026. This investment will enable the CAF to defend the Arctic, including through infrastructure upgrades such as airfield improvements, new or repurposed hangars, ammunition and fuel facilities, and buildings and equipment for accommodations.  Given the timing of the Project’s construction, the MVH is expected to precede many of the major defence-related projects in the Northwest Territories. The Project could thus support construction activities associated with northern and Arctic defence infrastructure development. The Project would also provide important future logistical and operational benefits for the CAF in Canada’s North and Arctic region by enabling more efficient and reliable transportation for troops, equipment, and supplies.  Relatedly, the MVH aligns with the Government of Canada’s Plan for a Stronger Canada, released in October 2026. The plan includes a focus on exercising Canada’s sovereignty through a robust, permanent presence in the Arctic, as well as securing the country’s sovereignty in key sectors and delivering resources and expertise to the world.   Indigenous governments and organizations consulted by MPO expressed a range of perspectives regarding the Project’s potential to strengthen Canada’s autonomy, resilience, and security. Many Indigenous governments and organizations highlighted the strategic importance of the project in strengthening Canada’s northern presence and addressing Arctic sovereignty through connectivity, enhanced emergency preparedness, and reduced dependency on increasingly unreliable winter road systems. Several groups noted that the Project would provide a second road access route to the Beaufort Delta and Western Arctic region, reducing dependency on the existing Dempster Highway corridor. Many groups emphasized that resilience and security objectives should not be pursued at the expense of Aboriginal or treaty rights or existing regulatory and co-management frameworks.   Considering these points, the GIC has determined that the MVH would have a positive long-term impact on the resilience of isolated communities along the proposed route. In addition to strengthening supply chains and improving overall access for residents, the Project also provides meaningful support for Canada’s defence and sovereignty objectives, supporting an expanding Canadian military presence in the Northwest Territories and Canadian Arctic. Recognizing the need for continued Indigenous input to inform the Project’s planning and development, the MVH’s ability to support Canada’s autonomy, resiliency, and sovereignty is one of the Project’s most pronounced benefits.   Provides economic or other benefits to Canada   The GIC has concluded that the Project would generate direct and indirect economic benefits to Canada. As a major infrastructure project and public highway, the Project would support economic growth as well as improve affordability for communities in the Mackenzie Valley by providing year-round overland access for community resupply and other critical goods, as well as supporting increased tourism. The Project would also help to facilitate access to the exploration and development of important natural resources in the region that have key industrial, defence, and energy applications. Finally, the MVH is expected to provide important employment, training, and social benefits for residents in communities along the route.  The MVH is a major capital project that would represent a significant investment in the Northwest Territories and for Canada more broadly. As a large infrastructure project, the MVH would have a substantial impact on Territorial GDP, and at its peak MPO estimates approximately 3,000 workers would be directly employed to build the project. Economic benefits would include direct employment, training, contracting and subcontracting activity, as well as indirect activities that occur through the Project’s development, construction and post-construction operations and maintenance.   The MVH is expected to create good-paying jobs, increase economic activity, and contribute to GDP growth. Employment would be generated across disciplines such as construction, engineering, equipment operation, materials transportation and logistics planning, lodging, and environmental services. Post-construction operation and maintenance of the highway is expected to sustain local jobs after the Project is complete for activities such as road maintenance and repairs. Predictable employment would also have positive indirect effects for the economic and socio-economic development of Northwest Territories communities.   Investments in transportation infrastructure such as roads enable economic growth by reducing transportation costs, connecting communities, and strengthening supply chains. Better access to roads also improves access to vehicles, machinery, and equipment. This is relevant in the context of the Project, given that the Mackenzie Valley and Beaufort Delta regions, which would be connected by the new highway, contain substantial natural resource potential.   The MVH could therefore support increased future mineral and energy exploration and development activity by providing access to known resources, such as zinc, copper, cobalt, rare earths, and oil and gas resources. These resources have a wide range of applications, and notably are critical inputs to support energy production, manufacturing, technological applications, and national defence. Specifically, the Project would reduce transportation costs by providing year-round ground transportation for equipment, supplies, and cargo exports, and reducing dependence on barges and aircraft. By improving overall access to remote areas, the Project would enable greater year-round exploration activity, which would be an important benefit for Canada.  In addition to expanding resource potential, the MVH would enable additional trade between regions within the Northwest Territories, and with other provinces and territories. The highway would facilitate increased imports of food, fuel and consumer goods, as well as capital goods for highway construction and maintenance. The Project is expected to reduce the cost per tonne of freight into the area, which could induce new development. Finally, the Project is expected to encourage new tourism activity by creating a scenic driving route through the Northwest Territories and Yukon in combination with the Dempster Highway. This could bolster and induce the development of new tourism businesses in communities along the MVH route.   Beyond economic benefits, the GIC has considered that the Project would yield important benefits for communities located along the highway route. In general, communities with road access have lower food prices than communities that are not connected with four-season roads. Mackenzie Valley communities, particularly in the Sahtu region, face some of the highest costs of living in Canada, largely due to remoteness and lack of reliable transportation links. Improved road access could help to stabilize the cost of essential goods and services, generating savings by reducing transportation time and associated operating costs. New four-season road access would also allow Mackenzie Valley residents to more easily travel to other communities, including regional hubs such as Inuvik and Fort Simpson, to access medical and other government services and for personal reasons.   Indigenous governments and organizations consulted by MPO identified a range of potential economic benefits associated with the project including employment, contracting and procurement opportunities, reduced transportation costs, tourism growth, lower costs of living, and reliable access to goods and services for northern communities. Some Indigenous governments and organizations also noted the Project's potential to enable increased access to resource development opportunities.   Many noted that meaningful economic reconciliation requires more than short term employment opportunities, highlighting the importance of Indigenous participation, benefit-sharing mechanisms, and preferential access to procurement opportunities. Indigenous governments and organizations, as well as communities who have been engaged on the Project, further stressed the need for workforce development, training, and skills-readiness initiatives to ensure they are well positioned to access and sustain long-term economic benefits throughout the life of the Project.   Overall, the GIC has concluded the Project is expected to provide material direct and indirect economic and other benefits to Canada, as well as to northern and Indigenous communities, while bolstering economic sovereignty. The Project would contribute to job creation, training and skills development, GDP growth, and could catalyze future growth in tourism and exploration and development of the region’s natural resources. The Project would also have important community benefits by stabilizing the cost of living and improving transportation access for residents of remote communities.   Has a high likelihood of successful execution  The GIC has considered that while the Project’s scope and remote location will necessitate a robust execution plan and support from the Government of Canada, overall, the Project has a credible pathway to completion, assuming timely advancement of planned activities and, critically, approval following the MVEIRB environmental assessment process.  Major projects in the North are subject to a unique set of circumstances and considerations. This includes seasonal constraints related to mobilization of personnel and equipment, such as transport using winter roads or summer Mackenzie River barges, extensive permafrost requiring specialized construction techniques, challenging physical working conditions such as sustained cold and severe weather conditions, and limited resource and labour availability. Together, these considerations increase the complexity and costs associated with project advancement in the North.   The current formulation of the MVH has been in development since 2013, with various iterations of the proposed highway being studied since 1958. This history is reflected in the different levels of design, execution readiness and procurement status of the various MVH project components. While the northern section of the Project (from Norman Wells to the Dempster Highway south of Inuvik) is being refined, scope maturity for the southern section (from Wrigley to Norman Wells) is more advanced in development. This would facilitate the early start of construction for elements that are more “shovel ready,” with a phased approach to construction.   Importantly, the Project intends to largely replace the existing Mackenzie Valley Winter Road rather than establish an entirely new route, with some new routing in the Dehcho region and the Gwich’in Settlement Area between Fort Good Hope and Tsiigehtchic. Route refinement would continue as the Project advances from design stage towards construction.   The GNWT is the proponent and the MVH is intended to operate as a public territorial highway, with important defence and security benefits. The GNWT has relevant experience delivering northern highways in similar conditions, including the Inuvik-Tuktoyaktuk Highway, and the Tlicho All Season Road. However, the scale and timeframe for the MVH’s construction is significantly more complex than these past projects.  To that end, the Government of Canada will support the Project via a new major projects management entity. The entity will ensure the Project can access the expertise and resources required to move quickly. Once established, this purpose-built organization will have specialized technical and project management expertise to support major project development, including the identification and mitigation of risks.   Funding is a key consideration in relation to executability and there is significant value in providing upfront, predictable funding to deliver the entire route in an integrated manner. The Project’s northern and southern sections have an estimated capital cost of $4.2 billion. On September 8, 2026, the Government of Canada announced federal funding of $405 million through the Arctic Infrastructure Fund to support early-stage work on the Project, including to finalize routing and design, and initiate construction of the Great Bear River Bridge near Tulita. Further, on November 5, 2026, Budget 2026 proposed to fully fund the construction and certain maintenance costs of the MVH.   Through consultations, many Indigenous governments and organizations highlighted the recent history of similar highways built and maintained by the GNWT, while also reflecting on lessons learned from these projects. Many Indigenous governments and organizations noted that sustained capacity funding is required to enable groups to participate effectively in technical reviews, environmental monitoring, route planning, regulatory processes, and project governance. Indigenous governments and organizations noted that successful execution will also depend on developing long-term partnership and governance arrangements and including Indigenous Knowledge in decision making.  In summary, while the Project will face unique considerations given its scope and location, the GIC has concluded that Project progress to date and recent announcements through Budget 2026, including the establishment and funding of a new major projects management entity and a commitment to fully fund the construction and certain maintenance costs, support a high likelihood of successful execution.    Advances the interests of Indigenous peoples  The GIC has concluded that the Project advances the interests of Indigenous peoples.  As discussed more fully below in relation to Crown-Indigenous consultation, MPO conducted consultations with Indigenous governments and organizations in the Northwest Territories who may be impacted by the Project, seeking input on its proposed listing under the BCA. This dialogue and consultation would continue as the Project advances through the ongoing environmental assessment process and to inform the federal Conditions Document.   Pehdzeh Ki First Nation, the Gwich’in Tribal Council and Sahtu Secretariat Incorporated have signed a memorandum of understanding establishing a coordinated Indigenous approach to advancing the MVH. Together, these partners are seeking meaningful roles in project governance and decision-making to help ensure the highway delivers lasting benefits for their communities while avoiding, minimizing or mitigating adverse effects.   To that end, the three Indigenous governments, as well as the Government of Canada and the GNWT, have recently signed a Leadership and Governance Understanding agreement setting out arrangements for shared leadership and collaboration, including procurement and community readiness. The GNWT is advancing an MVH Community Readiness Strategy in collaboration with Indigenous governments, representative organizations and communities. The strategy addresses potential adverse effects and opportunities associated with highway construction and the transition to all-season access. Areas of focus include training and employment, road safety and security, socio-economic monitoring, and wildlife and fisheries considerations. Related community and business readiness work includes labour-market analysis and preparation for future procurement opportunities. Where possible, the Government of Canada will seek to support these GNWT-led efforts.  As a public use highway, the Project would not create direct revenue that could be shared, but the Proponent is committed to maximizing employment, training and contracting benefits for Indigenous peoples. The Project is expected to provide benefits to northern and Indigenous communities through employment, training, and contracting/subcontracting. Beyond the development and construction of the MVH, there would also be ongoing employment and contracting benefits from highway operation and maintenance for the full life of the highway.   Many Indigenous businesses and economic development corporations that operate in each of the communities along the proposed route already work on the annual construction and maintenance of the existing Mackenzie Valley Winter Road. The new major projects management entity would work in collaboration with Indigenous governments and organizations to ensure the procurement and contracting strategy reflects Indigenous interests and perspectives and encourage partnerships between Indigenous businesses and other companies engaged in the Project.  With respect to employment and training, many northern and Indigenous communities within the vicinity of the Project have high unemployment rates and there is a meaningful opportunity for the Project to support training and job creation for Indigenous peoples. Additional employment opportunities would exist related to highway operation and maintenance.  In addition to these direct benefits, the Project would also have positive impacts for the northern and Indigenous communities along the MVH by increasing access to reliable transportation. The Project would provide year-round road access to currently isolated communities where most travel is limited to flights or seasonal winter road access and reduce travel times to key regional hubs such as Inuvik and Yellowknife.  On balance, the GIC has concluded that the Project advances the interests of Indigenous peoples. The MVH would create a new four-season road that would benefit Indigenous peoples by providing material economic benefits through employment, training, and contracting. Input from Indigenous governments and organizations, including on important aspects like routing and community readiness, would continue to be sought through project development, as well as through the MVEIRB environmental assessment and to inform the federal regulatory review and Conditions Document.   Contributes to clean growth and to meeting Canada’s climate change objectives  The GIC has considered potential impacts of the Project on clean growth and on Canada’s climate objectives. Overall, the Project’s impacts on greenhouse gas emissions, which would occur through emissions related to construction activity and post construction operations and maintenance, are expected to be limited.   Further, the Project demonstrates potential to reduce certain emissions related to travel activity. Specifically, the Project would shorten the overland distance between the Northwest Territory’s two largest population centres, Yellowknife and Inuvik, by an estimated 1,300 kilometres, reducing fuel use and associated greenhouse gas emissions for travel by road. Year-round road access in the central Mackenzie Valley region is also expected to displace some higher-emitting air traffic currently used to move people and freight into communities without existing four-season road access.   At the same time, the Project would advance climate adaptation and resiliency objectives. Climate change adaptation includes actions that reduce the negative impacts of climate change or take advantage of potential new opportunities, thereby increasing resilience to a changing climate.   As Canada’s North and Arctic region is warming at a significantly faster rate relative to the rest of Canada, there is a need for more resilient transportation and adaptation measures that reduce the impacts of climate change on the region’s transportation infrastructure. Across the territories, northern and Indigenous communities are experiencing adverse impacts from climate change including shorter winter road seasons, changing ice conditions, and lower water levels, which can impact critical transportation networks that support the movement of people, goods, and services in the region.   The Project would support adaptation by replacing the Mackenzie Valley Winter Road, reducing reliance on seasonal ice crossings, which are increasingly vulnerable to changing climate conditions, and barge service across major rivers in the region, which are increasingly prone to disruption as river water levels fluctuate.   Indigenous governments and organizations consulted by MPO generally noted that the Project would support climate adaptation and enhance transportation reliability and community resilience. Groups highlighted that climate-related impacts on winter roads and river transportation affect the movement of goods, fuel, and supplies to northern communities. Indigenous governments and organizations also noted the need for additional information regarding greenhouse gas emissions, cumulative effects, induced development, wildlife impacts, habitat fragmentation, and permafrost degradation to generally assess the potential impact on clean growth and climate change.   The GIC has carefully weighed these considerations and concluded the Project is expected to support climate resiliency and adaptation, which are important components of Canada’s climate strategy. Emissions generated by the Project through construction, maintenance, and operation are expected to be limited and would be balanced against reduced emissions from the creation of a shorter route between key municipalities and reduced air travel. The GIC also notes the concerns of Indigenous peoples consulted and recognizes that the environmental assessment process carried out by the MVEIRB will provide a comprehensive review of project-specific and cumulative impacts, informing the identification of mitigation measures and any conditions that can be addressed through federal authorities with respect to potential effects on climate, ecosystems, and northern communities.    Terrestrial and aquatic environmental impacts  In addition to the five national interest factors explicitly contemplated in the Act, the GIC has considered the potential effects of the Project on terrestrial and aquatic environmental impacts. It has done so based on the currently available information, recognizing that the same impacts are being assessed concurrently through the MVEIRB environmental assessment.   During consultations, Indigenous governments and organizations expressed concerns regarding potential effects from the Project on wildlife populations such as moose and boreal caribou, fish and fish habitat, migratory species, water quality, wetlands, harvesting areas, travel routes, cabins, traplines, and culturally significant landscapes. Groups also noted concern surrounding increased access to the area and the additional pressures on terrestrial and aquatic populations, including impacts from construction and operation of the highway altering wildlife movement patterns, habitat fragmentation, and expanded access to previously remote areas that result in increased harvesting pressures.   While overall comments received in response to the publication of the Notice in the Canada Gazette were limited, submissions reiterated the importance of rigorously assessing and addressing potential environmental effects.  To reduce new terrestrial disturbances, the Project is expected to follow the existing Mackenzie Valley Winter Road corridor wherever possible. This approach would help limit the extent of new habitat fragmentation and disturbance by concentrating development within an already established transportation corridor. The Project is anticipated to require a relatively narrow footprint concentrated within a 60-metre right-of-way along the approximately 800 kilometre route, limiting the amount of surrounding land that would be disturbed. However, this design approach and its effectiveness in reducing environmental impacts will be assessed through the MVEIRB environmental assessment.  The MVH is likely to have impacts on permafrost, as it runs through areas with both continuous and discontinuous permafrost. Without careful management, road construction and operation could lead to permafrost degradation, including slumping or other destabilizing changes. Tools and lessons learned from recent comparable projects, such as the Inuvik-Tuktoyaktuk Highway and the Tlicho All-Season Road, can be leveraged to identify sensitive areas and aid in determining mitigation actions for precise route determination as well as construction techniques to avoid or mitigate permafrost degradation. The Project would also be advanced alongside broader initiatives aimed at protecting biodiversity, conserving habitat, and supporting sustainable development, such as the Government of Canada’s 2026 Strategy to Protect Nature, which provide vital context for assessing and mitigating potential environmental effects associated with major infrastructure projects.   The GIC has carefully weighed these considerations alongside the resiliency, economic, and sovereignty benefits of the Project. The GIC has considered that the MVH remains subject to comprehensive reviews by co-management boards under the MVRMA, which are responsible for determining whether impacts can be effectively mitigated and under what conditions. These assessments will draw on technical studies, traditional knowledge, and community feedback with findings informing project design, mitigation measures, monitoring programs, and regulatory decision-making. The outcomes of these processes would support the preparation of the Conditions Document to ensure that the Project’s risks are fully understood, transparently assessed, and mitigated through federal authorizations. Together, these processes provide a robust framework to ensure that potential environmental effects are rigorously assessed and addressed.   Crown-Indigenous Consultation   Overview  The Government of Canada is committed to advancing reconciliation, founded on the recognition of rights, respect, cooperation, and partnership. Consistent with this commitment, implementation of the BCA requires meaningful consultation and engagement with Indigenous peoples throughout project planning and decision-making processes.   Canada’s duty to consult with Indigenous governments and organizations on the possibility of listing a project, which is assigned to the responsible Minister under s. 5(7) of the Act, focuses on ensuring that the GIC is informed by and accounts for the potential impacts of a listing decision on the Aboriginal or treaty rights of Indigenous peoples. The Government of Canada remains committed to upholding the honour of the Crown, fulfilling its duty to consult and, where appropriate, accommodate, while implementing the principles reflected in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act and respecting modern treaties.   The GIC has concluded that the listing of the Project under the Act will not result in any adverse impacts to established or asserted Aboriginal or treaty rights. The listing of the Project under the Act does not authorize Project construction, constitute Project approval, or prescribe Project-specific mitigation measures. Consideration of potential Project impacts will continue to be assessed through the MVEIRB environmental assessment, which considers project impacts, identifies mitigation measures, as appropriate, and recommends whether the Project should proceed, and if so, under what conditions. The Conditions Document would address MVEIRB conditions that require federal authorizations for statutes listed under Schedule 2 of the Act.   In response to the publication of the Notice in the Canada Gazette, some comments emphasized the importance of continuing direct consultation for regulatory decisions that potentially affect Aboriginal or treaty rights and interests, while ensuring that appropriate capacity funding is provided to ensure meaningful participation.  The GIC is satisfied that the pre- and post-listing regulatory processes and attendant duty of consultation have ensured, and in the future will ensure, that any release of federal permits and authorizations will be consistent with the Honour of the Crown, and that any regulatory decisions on the Project have and will continue to be informed by meaningful consultation at each point of decision-making.   In reaching this determination, the GIC has considered the consultation process completed with Indigenous peoples, including meaningful two-way dialogue on issues raised, as summarized below.   Consultation Process   The consultation process with Indigenous governments and organizations was informed by the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and the principle of free, prior and informed consent. Consistent with Canada’s approach to implementation of the UN declaration, consultation seeks to reach mutually acceptable arrangements with Indigenous governments and organizations, with the aim of achieving consensus, where possible.   On June 24, 2026, on behalf of the responsible Minister, MPO issued notification letters, initiating consultation with 31 potentially impacted Indigenous governments and organizations regarding the potential listing of the Project under the BCA.   Consultation was undertaken between June 24, 2026 and October 1, 2026, and sought to understand Indigenous perspectives regarding the listing of the Project under the BCA and the factors supporting a listing decision, as well as understanding how a listing decision could affect established or asserted Aboriginal or treaty rights.   Consultation activities included notification letters, virtual and in-person meetings, information sessions, telephone discussions, receipt of written submissions, and ongoing correspondence. Funding was made available to support Indigenous governments’ and organizations’ participation throughout the listing consultation process. MPO also worked closely with federal partners, including the Canadian Northern Economic Development Agency’s Northern Projects Management Office and Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada, to inform consultation activities and support work to identify potentially affected Indigenous groups.   Both in-person and virtual meetings were held with Indigenous governments and organizations identified on the consultation list and with additional representative organizations and communities that requested information regarding the Project. Over the consultation period, MPO held 37 meetings with Indigenous governments and organizations. Of the 31 groups consulted, 13 Indigenous governments and organizations accessed capacity funding for the listing consultation process.   The consultation period occurred during the 2026 summer months, when many Indigenous communities were engaged in harvesting activities, cultural gatherings, community events, wildfire evacuations and response, and other seasonal priorities, impacting some communities’ capacity to participate. In response to these concerns, MPO offered an additional week to submit comments and continued to receive, review, and assess written submissions after October 1, 2026.   MPO received 14 written submissions from potentially impacted Indigenous governments and organizations as of November 23, 2026. MPO reviewed and developed initial Crown responses to matters that had been raised in meetings or through written submissions. On November 9 and 10, 2026, MPO provided participating Indigenous governments and organizations with draft community consultation summaries and initial Crown responses for their review and validation and invited communities to identify any inaccuracies, omissions, or clarifications to ensure that concerns, interests, and perspectives were accurately reflected in the consultation record and understood by Canada.   To facilitate participation in the consultation process, MPO employed multiple consultation mechanisms, including:  participant funding for all rights holding governments and organizations;bilateral meetings conducted both virtually and in-person;regional virtual information sessions on the BCA, its applications in the Northwest Territories, and on the MVH;ongoing correspondence and two-way follow-up discussions; responses to community questions and information requests;opportunities for Indigenous governments and organisations to review draft community consultation summaries before finalization in MPO’s consultation report; and opportunities to provide written submissions.  Senior MPO officials participated directly in consultation activities and made themselves available for meetings when requested. These officials remained available throughout the consultation period to provide the best available information, answer questions, and discuss concerns raised by Indigenous governments and organizations.    Views Expressed During Consultation  Indigenous governments and organizations expressed a broad range of views regarding both the Project and its potential listing under the BCA. While opinions differed on whether to list the Project, there was widespread recognition of the MVH’s importance for the Northwest Territories. Many Indigenous governments and organizations acknowledged the potential benefits associated with improved year-round road access, reduced transportation costs, increased affordability of goods and services, enhanced emergency response capabilities, improved transportation reliability, economic development opportunities, workforce development, Indigenous business participation, increased tourism, and broader support for Arctic sovereignty and northern resilience.   At the same time, Indigenous governments and organizations consistently emphasized that support for the Project or its listing should not be interpreted as unconditional support for the Project including important future processes like routing decisions, regulatory approvals, or federal authorizations. Many communities stressed that meaningful consultation, protection of Aboriginal and Treaty rights, Indigenous participation in project governance and decision-making, and respect for existing treaty-based regulatory and co-management processes all remain essential prerequisites for project advancement.  Below is a more detailed description of consultation feedback by theme.   Indigenous Rights, Governance, Participation, and Project Decision-Making    Protection of Indigenous rights was a central theme throughout consultation. Indigenous governments and organizations emphasized the importance of respecting treaty rights, Aboriginal rights, and existing co-management and regulatory regimes. Many Indigenous governments and organizations emphasized the need for meaningful involvement in project governance, monitoring, oversight, and future decision-making processes, including through the incorporation of Indigenous Knowledge.  Many Indigenous governments and organizations also identified capacity funding and consultation resources as essential to supporting informed participation throughout the BCA process and subsequent regulatory reviews. Questions were raised regarding the definition and application of "national interest”, the implications of listing under the BCA, and whether listing could create perceptions of a predetermined outcome. Indigenous governments and organizations sought greater clarity regarding how the BCA would interact with existing regulatory and environmental assessment processes in the Northwest Territories, such as those established under the MVRMA, and emphasized that future consultation and regulatory reviews must continue to provide meaningful opportunities to identify, assess, and address impacts on Indigenous rights and interests.   Project Development, Route Planning, and Strategic Outcomes   Indigenous governments and organizations noted that the limited project information available constrained their ability to assess potential impacts and benefits. They requested additional clarity regarding route alignments, engineering design, construction approaches, environmental considerations, and long-term project planning. Concerns were raised regarding route uncertainty, particularly where potential alignments could affect culturally important areas, harvesting locations, or community interests. Participants emphasized the need for ongoing communications, community liaison mechanisms, community and elder input on routing decisions, and transparent information sharing throughout project development.   Indigenous governments and organizations considered the Project within the broader context of climate change, declining winter-road reliability, permafrost degradation, transportation resilience, affordability, and the high cost of living in northern communities. Many participants recognized the Project’s potential contribution to Arctic sovereignty, northern security, strategic infrastructure development, and long-term regional connectivity, while stressing that these potential benefits must be balanced with the protection of Indigenous rights and interests.   Community Well-Being and Socio-economic Effects   Indigenous governments and organizations emphasized the importance of ensuring that communities along the proposed route are prepared to benefit from project-related opportunities. Participants highlighted the need for training, education, skills development, and workforce readiness initiatives to support meaningful Indigenous participation in future employment and contracting opportunities.   Many Indigenous governments and organizations raised expectations regarding Indigenous ownership, revenue-sharing arrangements, and other long-term economic benefits. They also expressed concerns that increased road access could contribute to drug and alcohol trafficking, crime, and other social challenges. Many stressed that existing health, social service, policing, and emergency response capacities in many communities are already strained and may require significant enhancement to address increased use of the highway. Housing shortages, infrastructure pressures, community safety, and the need for adequate monitoring, enforcement, and emergency response measures were also frequently identified as priorities.   Environmental Stewardship and Land Use   Indigenous governments and organizations consistently voiced the importance of protecting lands, waters, wildlife, and traditional harvesting activities. Concerns were raised regarding potential effects on hunting, fishing, trapping, gathering, and access to country foods, as well as the possibility that the highway could increase pressure from non-locals on resources relied upon by Indigenous communities.   Participants also identified concerns regarding impacts to water resources, gravel sources, wildlife habitat, permafrost degradation, culturally significant sites, and areas of ecological importance. Several Indigenous governments and organizations emphasized the need to understand cumulative effects in the context of historical, existing, and reasonably foreseeable future development, and stressed the importance of Indigenous stewardship, monitoring, and environmental protection measures throughout project planning and implementation.   GIC Assessment  The GIC is satisfied that the consultation process has provided a meaningful opportunity for Indigenous governments and organizations to share their views on potential adverse impacts on established or asserted Aboriginal and treaty rights, communicate community-specific concerns, priorities, and recommendations, and inform the GIC's understanding of Indigenous perspectives regarding the potential implications of a listing decision. Through the consultation process, the GIC obtained a substantial understanding of the issues and concerns Indigenous governments and organizations consider most significant with respect to the proposed listing.  The GIC acknowledges the concerns raised regarding potential project impacts on Aboriginal and treaty rights, the environment, traditional land use, socio-economic conditions, and community well-being. Listing under the BCA does not amend the treaty-based assessment process in the Northwest Territories, or the Crown’s duty to consult and accommodate regarding potential impacts of the Project on Aboriginal or treaty Rights. The GIC takes assurance that assessments under the Territories’ co-management regime, including the current environmental assessment process, will ensure environmental and socio-economic impacts are appropriately addressed. The outcome of the environmental assessment, along with continued consultation and consideration of potential impacts on rights, will also inform any subsequent conditions development process under the BCA.   Further, the GIC recognizes the importance of ensuring Indigenous perspectives, Indigenous Knowledge, and community priorities are considered throughout project planning, assessment, and decision-making processes and where applicable, project implementation and monitoring. The GIC also acknowledges that meaningful participation in regulatory and consultation processes requires sufficient capacity and resources.   The GIC recognizes the strong interest of Mackenzie Valley Indigenous Governments meaningfully participating in project governance and decision-making, as evidenced by the recent the signing of the Mackenzie Valley Highway Leadership Governance Understanding. This document will create a durable framework for shared project leadership and decision-making.   The GIC acknowledges concerns regarding community readiness, including local capacity constraints, housing, infrastructure and health and social service pressures, workforce training and availability, community safety, and access to employment and business opportunities.   The GNWT is advancing an MVH Community Readiness Strategy with Indigenous governments, communities and relevant departments to identify and address potential project-related effects during construction and following the introduction of all-season access. The strategy will include measures to avoid, minimize or mitigate adverse effects, support training and employment, prepare northern and Indigenous businesses for procurement opportunities, and monitor socio-economic outcomes so that responses can be adjusted as needed.  Finally, the GIC appreciates the significant efforts made by Indigenous governments, organizations, Elders, and community members to participate in consultation activities despite competing demands, capacity constraints, seasonal activities, wildfire impacts, and ongoing involvement in the MVEIRB environmental assessment. The views, concerns, recommendations, and Indigenous Knowledge shared throughout consultations informed the Government's consideration of whether the Project should be listed as a project of national interest under the BCA.  In light of these points, the GIC is satisfied that the post-BCA listing treaty-based assessment processes will provide an appropriate framework through which these concerns can be meaningfully examined and considered prior to the issuance of a Conditions Document.  Next Steps Following listing of the Project, MPO will participate in the MVEIRB environmental assessment alongside other federal departments and agencies, as part of its role supporting responsible ministers under the MVRMA. In this capacity, MPO will use the stages of the environmental assessment, including the information request phase and technical reviews, to ensure that federal regulatory requirements, authorization considerations, and potential implementation issues are identified and assessed as part of the MVEIRB environmental assessment.  This work would support preparedness for the efficient development of the Conditions Document, informed by the MVEIRB environmental assessment, should the Project ultimately receive the necessary approvals. The Conditions Document would replace individual federal permits and authorizations for statutes listed under Schedule 2 of the BCA that are required for the Project. The Conditions Document would be issued following the completion of the MVEIRB environmental assessment and associated MVRMA decision-making processes.   MPO, on behalf of the Minister, through its engagement with the GNWT, will continue to support territorial efforts with respect to the Project.   Conclusion In reaching a decision that the Project is in the national interest, the GIC considered the factors in subsection 5(6) of the Act, information gathered through consultation with Indigenous peoples, input from Canadians provided in response to the Canada Gazette Notice, and engagement with the GNWT and federal departments, among other factors and sources of information. The GIC is satisfied that the duty to consult with Indigenous peoples in relation to the listing decision has been fulfilled. The GIC is further assured that consultations with Indigenous peoples will continue as part of the ongoing MVEIRB environmental assessment following the listing of the Project under the Act. Information gathered through these processes, including the final recommendations detailed in the MVEIRB’s Report of Environmental Assessment, will support the development and issuance of a Conditions Document should the Project receive necessary approvals to proceed.  The GIC has determined that the Project would materially strengthen Canada’s autonomy, resilience, security, and sovereignty while creating economic and other benefits that would support economic growth, improve affordability and connect communities in the Northwest Territories. Notably, the Project would provide material support for Canada’s defence and sovereignty objectives, enabling a stronger Canadian military presence in the Canadian Arctic and the development of vital national infrastructure. The Project also demonstrates a credible pathway for successful execution with a dedicated major projects management entity, and it is expected to provide benefits to Indigenous peoples and advance their interests through the establishment of a new public-use highway, as well as through employment, training and contracting opportunities. The Project would strengthen climate resiliency and adaptation, while its impacts on greenhouse gas emissions are expected to be limited. Although the Project is anticipated to have some adverse impacts on terrestrial and aquatic environments, the GIC has concluded that these impacts can be mitigated through regulatory review processes, established under the MVRMA, including the ongoing environmental assessment, and do not displace the national interest character of the Project.   Having regard to the considerations above, the GIC is of the view that the Mackenzie Valley Highway is in the national interest, and has, by Order, amended Schedule 1 to add the name of the Project and a detailed description of it.
